solution:
A sugar gives a positive Tollens test only if it is a reducing sugar, that is, only if it still carries a free hemiacetal group. Section 14.2.7 explains why : the hemiacetal group of a glucopyranose ring is a potential aldehyde group, and it is this group that imparts reducing properties and gives the positive Tollens and Fehling tests.

In sucrose the glycosidic linkage is formed between C-1 of \(\alpha\)-glucose and C-2 of \(\beta\)-fructose (Fig. 14.8). C-1 of glucose is its anomeric (hemiacetal) carbon and C-2 of fructose is its anomeric (hemiketal) carbon, so the potential aldehyde group of the glucose unit and the potential ketone group of the fructose unit are BOTH used up in making the bond. Neither unit has a free hemiacetal group left, so sucrose is a non-reducing sugar and gives a negative Tollens test.

In maltose the two \(\alpha\)-D-glucose units are joined by an \(\alpha\)-1,4-glycosidic linkage : C-1 of the first ring bonds to C-4 of the second (Fig. 14.9). C-4 is an ordinary alcoholic hydroxyl, so the hemiacetal group at C-1 of the second ring is not involved in the linkage and stays free. That free hemiacetal group can open to a potential aldehyde group, so maltose is a reducing sugar and gives a positive Tollens test.

DNA is double stranded (section 14.4.3). The two polynucleotide strands are held to each other by hydrogen bonding between the bases, and the pairing is fixed : adenine always forms two hydrogen bonds with thymine, and guanine forms three hydrogen bonds with cytosine, so A - T and C - G are complementary base pairs and the two strands are complementary to each other.

Because the pairing is strictly A with T, every adenine in the double helix stands opposite one thymine and every thymine stands opposite one adenine. There can be no unpaired base in the helix, so the number of adenine units in a DNA molecule must equal the number of thymine units. Complete hydrolysis breaks the polynucleotide down into its bases without altering how many of each there were, so the adenine and thymine released come out in equimolar quantities.

(By the same argument guanine and cytosine are also released in equimolar quantities.)

Section 14.3.1 states that \(\alpha\)-amino acids are high melting, water soluble crystalline solids, unlike simple amines or carboxylic acids, and that these properties are due to the zwitter ion structure.

An \(\alpha\)-amino acid molecule carries an acidic carboxyl \(\mathrm{-COOH}\) group and a basic amino \(\mathrm{-NH_2}\) group in the same molecule. A proton passes from the acidic group to the basic group, so the molecule exists not as a neutral covalent molecule but as an internal salt, the dipolar zwitter ion \(\mathrm{H_3N^{\oplus}-CHR-COO^{\ominus}}\) (Fig. 14.15). In the solid the crystal is therefore built of full positive and full negative charges held by strong electrostatic (ion-ion) forces, essentially an ionic lattice. A great deal of energy is needed to break that lattice down, so the melting point is high.

A simple amine or a simple carboxylic acid of comparable molecular mass has only one of the two groups, cannot transfer a proton internally, and stays a neutral molecule held in the solid by much weaker dipole-dipole and hydrogen-bonding forces, so it melts far lower. The chapter's own comparison on printed page 309 makes the size of the effect plain : alanine \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(NH_2)-COOH}\), molecular mass 89, melts at \(293.5^\circ\mathrm{C}\), whereas \(\mathrm{C_5H_{11}-NH_2}\) (molecular mass 87) melts at \(-55^\circ\mathrm{C}\) and \(\mathrm{C_3H_7-COOH}\) (molecular mass 88) at \(-7.9^\circ\mathrm{C}\).

Sucrose itself is dextrorotatory, its specific rotation being \(+66.5^\circ\). On hydrolysis with dilute acid or with the enzyme invertase it gives an equimolar mixture of D-(+)-glucose and D-(-)-fructose (section 14.2.9 a).

The two products rotate the plane of polarised light in opposite senses, and they do not cancel : the laevorotation of fructose, \(-92.4^\circ\), is larger in magnitude than the dextrorotation of glucose, \(+52.7^\circ\). The equimolar mixture therefore has a net LAEVOrotation.

So the hydrolysis has inverted the sign of the optical rotation of the solution, from dextro \((+66.5^\circ)\) for sucrose to laevo for the product mixture. It is this inversion of the sign of rotation that gives the reaction its name : the hydrolysis of sucrose is called inversion of sucrose, and the product mixture is called invert sugar.

Egg albumin is a globular protein (section 14.3.3 a) and, like other globular proteins, it is folded with its hydrophobic side chains tucked into the interior and its polar residues on the outside, which is what makes it water soluble.

Boiling denatures it. Section 14.3.5 states that high temperature, acid, base and even agitation disrupt the noncovalent interactions responsible for the specific shape of a protein, and that denaturation changes the molecular shape of the protein WITHOUT breaking the amide/peptide bonds that form the primary structure. So on boiling the secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure of egg albumin is disturbed - the hydrogen bonds, electrostatic attractions and London dispersion forces that held the chain coiled are destroyed - while the sequence of amino acid residues stays intact.

Uncoiling exposes the hydrophobic regions that were buried inside, and the chapter notes that this makes a denatured globular protein water insoluble. The uncoiled chains therefore aggregate and coagulate out of the aqueous white of the egg as a solid mass, which scatters light instead of transmitting it. That is why the clear, soluble albumin turns into an opaque white solid on boiling, and why the change is not reversed on cooling.

a. The polynucleotide is double stranded. — (DNA only). Section 14.4.3 gives the Watson and Crick model, in which DNA consists of two polynucleotide strands wound into a right-handed double helix, and the same section closes by noting that RNA exists as a single stranded structure.

b. The polynucleotide contains uracil. — (RNA only). Section 14.4.1 states that uracil (U) occurs only in RNA while thymine (T) occurs only in DNA.

c. The polynucleotide contains D-ribose. — (RNA only). In RNA the sugar component of the nucleotide unit is D-ribose, while in DNA it is 2-deoxy-D-ribose (section 14.4.1, Fig. 14.24).

d. The polynucleotide contains Guanine. — (both DNA and RNA). The Remember box in section 14.4.1 lists RNA as containing D-ribose with A, G, C, U and DNA as containing D-2-deoxyribose with A, G, C, T, so guanine is common to both.

The complementary strand runs in the opposite direction to the given strand, that is, from its own 3' end to its own 5' end, and its bases follow from the complementary base pairs A - T and C - G (section 14.4.3).

a. Original strand : 5' - C G T T T A A G - 3'

Complementary strand : 3' - G C A A A T T C - 5'

Written in the usual \(5' \rightarrow 3'\) sense the complementary strand is 5' - CTTAAACG - 3'.

b. Original strand : 5' - C C G G T T A A T A C G G C - 3'

Complementary strand : 3' - G G C C A A T T A T G C C G - 5'

Written in the usual \(5' \rightarrow 3'\) sense the complementary strand is 5' - GCCGTATTAACCGG - 3'.

A dipeptide is formed when the carboxyl group of one \(\alpha\)-amino acid combines with the amino group of another with loss of a water molecule, the two residues then being joined by a peptide bond (section 14.3.2, Fig. 14.17). The residue that keeps its free amino group is the N-terminal and is written on the left; the residue that keeps its free carboxyl group is the C-terminal and is written on the right (section 14.3.4 a). The N-terminal residue takes the ending -yl, which is why glycine + alanine in that order gives glycylalanine. Reversing the order gives a DIFFERENT compound, so order matters and each pair of amino acids yields two distinct dipeptides.

Using the three-letter symbols of Table 14.1 - Ala for alanine, Gly for glycine, Tyr for tyrosine - the schematic representations (Fig. 14.18 b) and names of the dipeptides in which the two residues are different are :

| Schematic representation | Name |
|---|---|
| Gly - Ala | glycylalanine |
| Ala - Gly | alanylglycine |
| Gly - Tyr | glycyltyrosine |
| Tyr - Gly | tyrosylglycine |
| Ala - Tyr | alanyltyrosine |
| Tyr - Ala | tyrosylalanine |

That is six dipeptides. If a dipeptide made of two molecules of the same amino acid is also counted, there are three more - Gly - Gly (glycylglycine), Ala - Ala (alanylalanine) and Tyr - Tyr (tyrosyltyrosine) - making nine in all. The chapter does not say which of the two readings is intended, so both counts are given here.

Section 14.2.4 establishes the formyl group in two steps, and either of the following pairs of observations is the evidence asked for.

1. Glucose contains a carbonyl group. Glucose reacts with hydroxylamine \(\mathrm{NH_2OH}\) to form an oxime, and with hydrogen cyanide \(\mathrm{HCN}\) to form a cyanohydrin. Only a carbonyl \(\mathrm{>C=O}\) group gives these two addition products, so glucose must contain one.

2. That carbonyl group is aldehydic, that is, a formyl group. Glucose is oxidised by bromine water, which is only a MILD oxidising agent, to gluconic acid \(\mathrm{COOH-(CHOH)_4-CH_2OH}\), a six-carbon monocarboxylic acid. A ketonic carbonyl is not attacked by so mild an oxidising agent, and oxidation without loss of a carbon shows the carbonyl carbon was already bearing a hydrogen atom. Hence the carbonyl group of glucose is a terminal \(\mathrm{-CHO}\), a formyl group.

A third piece of evidence from section 14.2.7 points the same way : glucose gives a positive Tollens test and a positive Fehling test, and these are tests for a (potential) aldehyde group.

The Haworth formula of glucopyranose is drawn in the accompanying diagram (Fig. 14.6 of the chapter).

Points to keep right while drawing it (section 14.2.6) :

- The pyranose ring is six membered - five carbons, C-1 to C-5, and one oxygen - and is drawn as though it were in a plane perpendicular to the plane of the paper, with the ring oxygen at the back right and C-1 at the right-hand end.

- The lower side of the ring is the \(\alpha\)-side and the upper side is the \(\beta\)-side.

- \(\mathrm{C\text{-}6}\), the \(\mathrm{-CH_2OH}\) group, is drawn above C-5.

- In \(\alpha\)-D-(+)-glucopyranose the anomeric hydroxyl group at C-1 points DOWN, on the \(\alpha\)-side; in \(\beta\)-D-(+)-glucopyranose it points UP, on the \(\beta\)-side. The two differ only in this.

- The remaining groups follow the rule that whatever appears on the right in the Fischer projection formula appears on the \(\alpha\)-side (below) in the Haworth formula, and vice versa : so \(\mathrm{-OH}\) is below at C-2, above at C-3 and below at C-4.

A zwitter ion is the dipolar ion formed when the proton of the acidic carboxyl group of an \(\alpha\)-amino acid is transferred to its own basic amino group, giving an internal salt that carries a full positive and a full negative charge but no net charge (section 14.3.1, Fig. 14.15) :

\(\mathrm{H_2N-CHR-COOH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{H_3N^{\oplus}-CHR-COO^{\ominus}}\)

So the structure to be drawn is

\(\mathrm{H_3N^{\oplus}-CHR-COO^{\ominus}}\)

in which the \(\mathrm{-COOH}\) group has become the carboxylate \(\mathrm{-COO^{\ominus}}\) and the \(\mathrm{-NH_2}\) group has become the ammonium \(\mathrm{-NH_3^{\oplus}}\), with R the side chain on the \(\alpha\)-carbon.

For a named example, the zwitter ion of alanine (Fig. 14.16, form A) is

\(\mathrm{H_3N^{\oplus}-CH(CH_3)-COO^{\ominus}}\)

This is the form in which a neutral \(\alpha\)-amino acid exists at about pH 6; at low pH \((\mathrm{pH} < 2)\) the carboxylate takes a proton to give the cation \(\mathrm{H_3N^{\oplus}-CH(CH_3)-COOH}\) of overall charge \(+1\), and at high pH \((\mathrm{pH} > 10)\) the ammonium group loses a proton to give the anion \(\mathrm{H_2N-CH(CH_3)-COO^{\ominus}}\) of overall charge \(-1\).

The Haworth formula of maltose is drawn in the accompanying diagram (Fig. 14.9 of the chapter).

Points to keep right while drawing it (section 14.2.9 b) :

- Maltose \(\mathrm{(C_{12}H_{22}O_{11})}\) is made of TWO units of D-glucose, so two six-membered pyranose rings are drawn side by side in Haworth form.

- The glycosidic bond joins C-1 of the left-hand ring to C-4 of the right-hand ring, through an ether oxide oxygen. The ring that uses its C-1 hydroxyl is \(\alpha\)-glucopyranose, so the C-1 oxygen leaves that ring on the \(\alpha\)-side (downwards) and the linkage is called an \(\alpha\)-1,4-glycosidic linkage.

- The hemiacetal group at C-1 of the SECOND (right-hand) ring is not used in the linkage and must be shown as a free \(\mathrm{-OH}\). This free hemiacetal is what makes maltose a reducing sugar.

- Each ring carries \(\mathrm{-CH_2OH}\) at C-6 above C-5, and hydroxyl groups at the remaining carbons.

The secondary structure of a protein is the three-dimensional arrangement of localized regions of the protein chain, and it arises from hydrogen bonding between the N-H proton of one amide linkage and the C=O oxygen of another. The two types commonly found in proteins are the \(\alpha\)-helix and the \(\beta\)-pleated sheet (section 14.3.4 b), and both are drawn in the accompanying diagram (Figs. 14.19 and 14.20 of the chapter).

\(\alpha\)-Helix - the polypeptide chain is twisted into a right handed (clockwise) spiral. Each turn of the helix has 3.6 amino acids; the C=O group of one amino acid is hydrogen bonded to the N-H group of the fourth amino acid along the chain; the hydrogen bonds run parallel to the axis of the helix and the R groups point outward from the helix core. Myosin in muscle and \(\alpha\)-keratin in hair are almost entirely \(\alpha\)-helical.

\(\beta\)-Pleated sheet - two or more polypeptide chains, called strands, line up side by side and are held together by hydrogen bonding. The C=O and N-H bonds lie in the plane of the sheet; hydrogen bonding occurs between the N-H and C=O groups of nearby residues in neighbouring chains; and the R groups are oriented above and below the plane of the sheet. This arrangement is favoured by amino acids with small R groups.

AMP is adenosine monophosphate, the nucleotide built from D-ribose, the purine base adenine and one phosphate group. Its structure is drawn in the accompanying diagram (from Fig. 14.27 of the chapter).

How it is put together (section 14.4.1) :

- Start with the five-membered furanose ring of D-ribose, which carries \(\mathrm{-OH}\) at both C-2' and C-3'. Primes are used on the sugar numbering to keep it distinct from the numbering of the base.

- Join the anomeric carbon C-1' of the ribose to the nitrogen at position 9 of adenine - the purine rule - which gives the nucleoside adenosine.

- Add a phosphate group to the 5'-OH of that nucleoside. A nucleotide is a monophosphate of a nucleoside, so this gives AMP.

The abridged name reads directly off the structure : the capital A is taken from the base adenine and MP stands for monophosphate. There is no small 'd' in front, so the sugar is ribose and not deoxyribose.

dAMP is deoxyadenosine monophosphate. It is built exactly like AMP except that the sugar is 2-deoxy-D-ribose instead of D-ribose. Its structure is drawn in the accompanying diagram (from Fig. 14.28 of the chapter).

How it is put together (section 14.4.1) :

- Start with the furanose ring of 2-deoxy-D-ribose. This is the sugar of DNA and it carries NO hydroxyl group at C-2' - that missing 2'-OH is the whole difference from AMP - while C-3' still carries its \(\mathrm{-OH}\).

- Join C-1' of the sugar to the nitrogen at position 9 of adenine, giving the deoxyribonucleoside deoxyadenosine.

- Add a phosphate group to the 5'-OH, which gives the nucleotide dAMP.

The abridged name again reads off the structure : the small letter 'd' at the beginning indicates deoxyribose in the nucleotide, A is for adenine and MP for monophosphate.

Of the five nitrogen-containing bases present in nucleic acids, two have two fused rings and are derived from the parent compound purine : adenine (A) and guanine (G) (section 14.4.1, Fig. 14.25). Either of them is an acceptable answer. The diagram accompanying this answer is the purine row of that figure - the parent compound purine with its ring numbering, and beside it the two purine bases adenine and guanine.

Adenine is purine carrying an amino \(\mathrm{-NH_2}\) group. Its skeleton is the purine bicycle - a six-membered pyrimidine ring fused to a five-membered imidazole ring, the ring atoms being numbered 1 to 9 - with the \(\mathrm{-NH_2}\) group on the six-membered ring and the N-H at position 9. It is position 9 that bonds to C-1' of the sugar when a nucleoside is formed from a purine base.

(Guanine, the other purine base, differs in carrying both an \(\mathrm{-NH_2}\) group and a \(\mathrm{>C=O}\) group on the six-membered ring. The three remaining bases - cytosine, uracil and thymine - have only one ring and are pyrimidine bases, so none of them would answer this question.)

Enzyme catalysis is described by the lock-and-key mechanism, drawn in the accompanying diagram (Fig. 14.23 of the chapter).

What the diagram must show, and why (section 14.3.6) :

- The enzyme, drawn with a notch of a particular size and shape on its surface. That notch is the ACTIVE SITE.

- The substrate, drawn so that it fits that notch. A substrate molecule can attach to the active site only if it has the right size and shape - this is what makes enzyme catalysis highly specific, so that an enzyme which hydrolyses an amide will not work on an ester or an acetal.

- The two joined together as the ENZYME - SUBSTRATE COMPLEX. Once in the active site the substrate is held in the correct orientation to react.

- The product leaving the active site, with the enzyme shown unchanged and ready to act as a catalyst again.

Formation of the enzyme-substrate complex has a very low activation energy, which is why the rate of the reaction is very high - some enzymes are so efficient that one enzyme molecule can catalyse the reaction of 10000 substrate molecules in one second.
